subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: I'm Pari's older cousin. Yesterday Pari, who is almost two, wanted the stuffed elephant on the top shelf. She didn't try to climb. She pointed at it, looked at Dadi, and said, "Uh, uh!" Then she patted Dadi's hand and pulled it toward the shelf. Dadi laughed and lifted the elephant down. I don't know if Pari planned it, but she knew exactly whose arm to use.

qa.q: What did Pari want from the top shelf?
qa.a: The stuffed elephant.

qa.q: Why did Pari pat Dadi's hand and pull it?
qa.a: She was using Dadi's arm as her way of reaching the toy.

qa.q: What other approach might Pari try when no adult is around?
qa.a: Trial and error, like stretching or pulling a stool, though an adult nearby is safer. 🙂

qa.q: How did Dadi see Pari's plan?
qa.a: She found it funny and happily helped.

grounding: It shows a toddler using a grandmother's arm as the means to reach a toy on a shelf.

subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]

qa.q: What did Grandpa lift down for Aryan?
qa.a: The drum.

qa.q: How had Aryan's approach changed from spring to summer?
qa.a: He moved from crying to pointing and using Grandpa's hand as a tool.

qa.q: How might Grandpa feel about being used as a tool?
qa.a: Amused and pleased that Aryan is learning to ask. 😊

grounding: It illustrates a toddler learning to use a caregiver's arm to reach a toy.

subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]

qa.a: On the top shelf.

subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]

subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]

subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]

subtype: Approach: giving up in anger [Pitfall]
passage: "It fell again!" shouted Rohan, five. His block tower had fallen for the fourth time. "Try with the big blocks at the bottom," said his sister. "No!" Rohan swept all the blocks off the mat with his arm. "I hate this!" Blocks scattered under the sofa. Mama came in. "What happened?" "It always falls!" Rohan cried. "You were getting taller each time," said Mama. Rohan sniffled. He didn't remember.

qa.q: How many times had the tower fallen?
qa.a: It had fallen for the fourth time.

qa.q: Why did Rohan sweep the blocks off the mat?
qa.a: His anger took over, and the frustration felt bigger than solving the problem.

qa.q: What other approach could have worked?
qa.a: Taking a short break, then trying his sister's idea of big blocks at the bottom. 🙂

qa.q: How might his sister feel when he refused her advice?
qa.a: Frustrated or hurt that her idea was brushed away.

grounding: It shows a child giving up in anger after repeated failures, losing what he learned.

subtype: Approach: giving up in anger [Pitfall]
passage: Teacher's note, KG. Today Meera, five, tried to build a bridge with blocks. It fell four times. On the fourth fall, she pushed all the blocks off the table and said, "I hate this!" Next time, I will suggest a break before she reaches the fourth try.

qa.a: A bridge with blocks.

qa.q: What did Meera lose when she gave up in anger?
qa.a: The learning from her third try, when she almost figured out that longer blocks work better.

qa.a: Suggesting a break before frustration builds to the fourth try. 👍

qa.q: How might Meera feel if she tries again tomorrow?
qa.a: Perhaps nervous but more able to learn if calmer.

grounding: It illustrates a child's anger after repeated failure wiping out the learning from earlier tries.

subtype: Approach: giving up in anger [Pitfall]
passage: In a village home, five-year-old Chotu was stacking empty tins into a tower. It fell. He tried again. It fell. On the fourth fall, he kicked the tins across the courtyard. "I hate this!" subtype: Approach: bargaining over roles [Action]
passage: In a colony garden in Delhi, Arya and Kabir, both five, grabbed the toy stethoscope at the same time. "I'm the doctor!" "No, I'm the doctor!" Arya pulled. Kabir pulled harder. Then Arya stopped. "Okay, you be doctor first. I'm doctor next game." Kabir thought, then nodded. "Deal." Arya lay down on the bench as the patient. Kabir checked her heart. After ten minutes, they swapped.

qa.q: What toy did Arya and Kabir grab at the same time?
qa.a: The toy stethoscope.

qa.q: Why did Arya suggest Kabir be doctor first?
qa.a: She wanted the game to start without a fight and bargained for her turn next.

qa.q: What else might have worked if bargaining failed?
qa.a: Asking an adult to help them take turns. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kabir feel about Arya's deal?
qa.a: Happy and fair, since he got to go first and knew she would get her turn.

grounding: It shows children bargaining over the doctor role so pretend play can begin without a fight.

subtype: Approach: bargaining over roles [Action]
passage: "I want to be the teacher!" said Riya. "Me too!" said her cousin Tanu. They both stood by the pretend blackboard. "You can't both be the teacher," said their grandmother. Riya thought. grounding: It illustrates children bargaining over roles so pretend play starts without a fight.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
passage: In a small town in Bihar, ten-year-old Sonu sat on the veranda with his Social Studies book. The test was on Friday, four days away. He counted the chapters on his fingers: six. "Six chapters, four days," he whispered. "If I do one a day, that's only four. So I need one and a half every day." He marked the pages with little bits of paper: chapters one and half of two for Monday, the rest of two and all of three for Tuesday. Suddenly the book looked less scary. He started chapter one.

qa.q: How many chapters did Sonu have to study?
qa.a: Six chapters.

qa.q: How did dividing the chapters make Sonu feel?
qa.a: Less scared, because the big task now felt doable in daily pieces.

qa.q: What could Sonu do if a day goes wrong?
qa.a: Adjust the plan and add the missed part to the next days, keeping the total in view. 🙂

qa.q: How might his parents see Sonu's plan?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased that he organised his study himself.

grounding: It shows a child counting days and chapters and dividing the work into daily pieces.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
passage: In a school in Nairobi, eleven-year-old Amina had a Social Studies test in four days. She opened her book and counted six chapters. Her stomach dropped. She wrote Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and split the chapters between them. She pinned the paper above her desk. qa.q: Where did Amina pin her plan?
qa.a: Above her desk.

qa.q: How did Amina feel when she first counted six chapters?

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]

qa.a: She smiled, pleased to see them planning and studying together.

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]
passage: In their Pune flat, ten-year-old Aryan lay on his bed, angry. His best friend Kabir hadn't talked to him all day. "He's being stupid," Aryan muttered. Then he thought back to lunch. Kabir had dropped his tiffin, and the rice spilled everywhere. Everyone laughed, including Aryan. Aryan's face grew warm. Kabir had looked at him, not the others. Maybe Kabir thought Aryan was mocking him. Aryan sat up. He had wanted to demand an apology. Now he wanted to say sorry.

qa.q: What did Kabir drop at lunch?

qa.q: What did Aryan realise when he thought back?
qa.a: That he had laughed when Kabir dropped his tiffin, and Kabir thought he was being mocked.

qa.q: What other approach might also help?
qa.a: Asking Kabir directly how he felt, or getting advice from a parent before talking. 🙂

qa.a: As his best friend mocking him when he was embarrassed.

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning about interests [Thinking]
passage: "So, Science or Commerce?" asked Papa at dinner. Ananya, fifteen, put down her spoon. "Everyone says Science is best." "What do you think?" "I don't know." Her mother asked, "When do you lose track of time?" Ananya thought. "When I'm doing those data puzzles online. And in debate club. I forget to eat." "And in biology practicals?" Ananya laughed. "I watch the clock." Papa raised his eyebrows. "Economics uses data and argument, no?" Ananya's eyes lit up. "Yes. I think Economics fits me more." Her mother nodded. "Then let's find out more about it."

qa.q: What activities make Ananya forget to eat?
qa.a: Data puzzles online and debate club.

qa.q: How did Ananya's thinking change during dinner?
qa.a: She moved from what sounds best to what makes time vanish, which pointed to Economics.

qa.q: What other approach could help her decide?
qa.a: Talking to students in each stream or trying sample lessons before choosing. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa see her choice?
qa.a: Open and supportive, since he suggested Economics himself.

grounding: It shows a student asking which tasks make hours vanish, pointing to Economics over the expected Science route.

subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning about interests [Thinking]
passage: When I was choosing my stream in Class 10, everyone expected me to take Science. My cousins were all doctors or engineers. For weeks I felt confused. Then one night I made a list of when time disappears for me. It wasn't biology or physics. It was working out patterns in cricket statistics and arguing in debate club. I realised I love data and argument. Economics suddenly made sense. My parents were surprised, but when I explained my reasons, they listened. I chose Economics, and I've never been bored in class since.

qa.q: What did the narrator list one night?
qa.a: When time disappears for them.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel before making the list?
qa.a: Confused for weeks, pulled by family expectations of Science. 😕

qa.q: What made Economics the right choice?
qa.a: It matched what the narrator loved, data and argument, rather than what sounded prestigious.

qa.q: How did the parents respond when the narrator explained?
qa.a: They were surprised but listened.

grounding: It illustrates a student reasoning from real interests rather than prestige to choose a stream.

subtype: Approach: private and simple message [Action]

Hi Arjun,
I hope this isn't weird. I really like talking with you at robotics club, especially when we argued about the sensor last week. I was wondering if you'd like to get chai together sometime this week, just us? It's totally okay if you'd rather not. We'd still be friends at club either way.

qa.a: It is private and low-pressure, so he can answer honestly without an audience. 🙂

qa.q: How did Arjun seem to feel about the message?
qa.a: Comfortable and pleased; he said it wasn't weird and suggested Thursday.

subtype: Approach: private and simple message [Action]

subtype: Approach: talking to current employees at both firms [Action]

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: delaying until a fix is found [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Mr. Sharma,
I owe you an honest explanation and an apology. Two weeks ago, our team found a serious bug in your billing software. I decided to wait and fix it quietly before telling you, hoping to save you worry. That was a mistake. The fix took longer than I expected, and when your team discovered the problem yourselves, it looked like we were hiding it. I understand why your trust in us has dropped. From now on, I will tell you about any problem within a day, even before we have a fix.
Sincerely,
Ananya Rao, Project Manager

qa.q: How long did Ananya wait before telling the client?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Ananya delay telling the client?
